title: Listen to an Announcement
lines: In this task one speaker gives an announcement or leaves a voicemail: a professor changing a class, a librarian explaining new rules, a coordinator describing a field trip, an office reminding students about a deadline. Each recording is about 70-130 words, followed by two questions.
## What is on the screen
- During the audio the screen may show a picture of the speaker or the place. No text of the announcement is shown.
- After the audio, two multiple-choice questions appear with four options each.
- You hear it once only. Notes are allowed.
## Timing
Listening lasts about 29 minutes in total, in two adaptive stages. Each announcement takes about 30-60 seconds to hear, then you answer quickly. Do not wait for a replay; there is none.
## What is being tested
- The purpose: why the announcement is being made (a change, a reminder, a warning, an invitation, new rules).
- Important details: new times, places, requirements, what to bring.
- What listeners must do, and by when.
- Sometimes an inference: who the announcement is for, or what will happen if listeners do nothing.
## How announcements are organized
Most announcements follow the same plan, which makes note-taking easy:
- Opening: who is speaking and to whom ("Good morning, everyone in Biology 101", "Hi Lucas, this is Olga from the housing office").
- Purpose: the main news, usually in the first or second sentence ("I'm calling because", "I want to let you know that", "Please note that").
- Details: what is changing, where, when, and why.
- Action: what listeners must do ("Please make sure", "You'll need to", "Remember to", "If you can't ..., then ...").
- Closing: thanks, contact information, or a reminder of the most important point.
## Method, step by step
- Step 1: Catch the speaker and the audience in the first seconds. This tells you the setting.
- Step 2: Write the main news in two or three words as soon as you hear it. This answers the purpose question.
- Step 3: Note details in a simple list: time, place, item, deadline. Write numbers carefully, and note any change ("was Rm 3, now Rm 12").
- Step 4: Listen for action language: must, need to, please, be sure to, don't forget, no later than.
- Step 5: Pay attention to the end. Speakers often repeat the key instruction there.
- Step 6: Answer from your notes. For purpose questions, choose the option that covers the main news, not a single detail.
## Worked example 1

> You hear (a professor): Good afternoon, everyone. Just a quick note before you leave. Next Wednesday's lab session won't take place in the usual lab, because the room is being repainted. Instead, we'll meet at the campus greenhouse behind the science building. We'll be measuring plant growth, so please wear closed shoes and bring the data sheet I'll post online tonight. Print it out, because there's no wifi in the greenhouse. If you have a class right before ours, don't worry about being a few minutes late; the walk takes about ten minutes.
> Question 1: What is the main purpose of the announcement?
> A. To explain how to measure plant growth
> B. To tell students about a change of location for a lab session
> C. To ask students to help repaint the lab
> D. To give directions to the science building
B states the main news. A is the activity, a detail. C misuses "repainted". D confuses the science building with the greenhouse, which is behind it.
> Question 2: What does the professor ask students to do?
> A. Download the data sheet in the greenhouse
> B. Arrive ten minutes early
> C. Bring a printed copy of a document
> D. Skip their class before the lab
C, from "Print it out". A is impossible because there is no wifi. B twists "the walk takes about ten minutes". D reverses his reassurance: they may be late, not skip a class.
## Worked example 2

> You hear (a voicemail): Hi Hamza, this is Priya from the Career Center. You signed up for a resume review this Friday at two. Unfortunately, the adviser you were booked with is away at a conference that day. We can move you to Monday at the same time with a different adviser, or you can keep Friday and do the session online with another colleague. Please call us back or reply to the confirmation email by Thursday noon so we can hold your place. Thanks!
> Question: What must Hamza do?
> A. Attend a conference on Friday
> B. Choose one of two options before a deadline
> C. Send his resume to the adviser by Monday
> D. Call the adviser who is away
B summarizes the request: pick Monday or online Friday, and reply by Thursday noon. A uses "conference" from the reason; C and D are not asked.
## Common traps
- A detail dressed as the purpose: the activity, the reason, or the location of something else.
- Reversed or mixed details: old room versus new room, the reason for a change versus the change.
- Numbers and times: the original time versus the new time, a duration versus a clock time.
- Words from the recording used with a different meaning or a different person.
! When you hear "instead", "now", "moved to" or "no longer", write the new information and cross out the old. Questions very often test the change.
## How to practise between mocks
- Listen to real announcements: university welcome videos, airport and station announcements, museum audio guides, recorded phone messages.
- After each one, write a three-line summary: purpose, key details, action required.
- Practise writing numbers, times and days quickly while listening; this is where many points are lost.
- Learn the language of instructions and requirements: mandatory, optional, required, in advance, at the latest, rescheduled, postponed.
